bug_description.original: OSS-Fuzz issue 42500437 (espeak-ng): Heap-use-after-free READ 1 found by fuzz target ssml-fuzzer [asan]. https://issues.oss-fuzz.com/issues/42500437
bug_description.original_source: sample_info.json / reproduction_report.json / sanitizer_trace.txt / patch.diff / staged vulnerable source under `_work/src/espeak-ng` / staged `poc` bytes
bug_description.normalized: The exact staged 10-byte witness `e2 80 af 24 e0 a5 a5 2b 9c 72` is passed to `ssml-fuzzer`, which copies it into a NUL-terminated string and feeds it to `espeak_Synth()` as UTF-8/SSML text. In vulnerable `Synthesize()`, `text_decoder_decode_string_multibyte(p_decoder, text, translator->encoding, flags)` materializes that attacker-controlled text into shared decoder state; `ReadClause()` then pulls it back out through `GetC()` to build `TranslateClause()`'s clause buffer and tokenized `sbuf`/`words[]` state. Because non-alpha punctuation is split unless it is in `punct_within_word` (default only `'`), the attacker-controlled word that reaches `TranslateWord2()` is a token selected from that tokenized buffer rather than simply the raw byte suffix after the leading separator. The initial translation of that selected word emits `phonSWITCH`, so `TranslateWord2()` calls `SetTranslator2(new_language)` and re-translates the same word through global `translator2`; AddressSanitizer's allocation stack shows the later-stale translator object was allocated through this call path. During that nested translation, `TranslateRules()` hits a later non-alphabetic character with no rule match and calls `LookupLetter(tr, wc, -1, ...)` while `tr` still aliases the live `translator2`. Vulnerable `LookupLetter()` probes English by calling `SetTranslator2("en")`, reusing the same global translator slot. The saved ASan free stack shows this nested call taking `SetTranslator2()`'s language-change branch and deleting the active `translator2` object. Control then returns to the outer `TranslateRules()` loop, which immediately dereferences the freed translator at `dictionary.c:2237` and crashes with the saved heap-use-after-free READ 1. The staged patch resolves this exact lifetime bug by moving nested fallback users in `numbers.c` onto separate `translator3` storage.

source.description: First project statement that consumes the attacker-controlled text and materializes it into decoder state later consumed by `GetC()` and `ReadClause()`.
source.value_from: The staged `poc` is exactly 10 bytes: `e2 80 af 24 e0 a5 a5 2b 9c 72`. `ssml-fuzzer` copies those bytes into a heap string, appends `str[size] = 0`, and calls `espeak_Synth()` with `espeakCHARS_UTF8 | espeakPHONEMES | espeakSSML`; this decode call is where project code first turns that witness into vulnerability-relevant project state.
source.note: Source step. `Synthesize()` decodes the fuzzer-provided UTF-8/SSML buffer into shared `p_decoder` state. `SpeakNextClause()` later drives `TranslateClause()` by pulling characters back out of this decoder, so this is the earliest project-side materialization on the crashing path.

root_cause.description: Nested `SetTranslator2("en")` reuses the same global `translator2` slot as the outer alternate-language translation. When the requested language differs, this branch frees the still-active translator object and clears the global, leaving the caller's live `tr` alias dangling.
root_cause.note: The staged patch fixes the bug by moving these nested fallback call sites onto independent `translator3` storage so this delete branch no longer tears down the outer translator.

sink.description: AddressSanitizer crash site. After the nested English fallback frees the active alternate translator, the outer `TranslateRules()` loop continues and dereferences freed translator memory through `tr->groups2_count[c]`.
sink.note: Stage 01's saved ASan trace reports a heap-use-after-free READ of size 1 at this exact line with stack `TranslateRules -> TranslateWord3 -> TranslateWord -> TranslateWord2`.

tainted_value_origin.description: The first translation of the attacker-derived word emits `phonSWITCH` plus an alternate-language string, turning the word into a nested-translator case.
tainted_value_origin.value_from: This state comes from the attacker-controlled word selected only after `Synthesize()` populates `p_decoder`, `ReadClause()` copies decoded characters into `source`/`charix`, and `TranslateClause()` tokenizes the clause into `sbuf`/`words[]`. Because `translate.c:2240-2246` splits unsupported punctuation and `2474-2504` finalizes each word span, the trace does not assume the whole byte suffix after the leading separator remained one word. The later ASan free stack proves the emitted outer `new_language` was not already `"en"`, because nested `SetTranslator2("en")` took the language-change delete branch.
tainted_value_origin.note: For this sample the first vulnerability-relevant derived state is not a size or index but the language-switch directive stored in `word_phonemes`: once `p[0] == phonSWITCH`, `TranslateWord2()` routes the same word through global `translator2` and sets up the stale-pointer lifetime hazard.

parser_admitted.description: After `Synthesize()` populates `p_decoder`, `ReadClause()` assembles the clause, and `TranslateClause()` tokenizes it, the selected word reaches `TranslateWord2()`, which is the entry point to the crashing translation logic.
parser_admitted.note: For the staged witness this call happens only after decoded characters have been copied out of `p_decoder` and tokenized into `sbuf`/`words[]`; unsupported punctuation is split at word boundaries, so the `word` argument here is an attacker-controlled token selected from `words[ix]`, not simply all bytes after the leading separator. That selected word is the one whose first translation emits `phonSWITCH` and whose retranslation later reaches `LookupLetter()`.

evidence_limitations: run_flags.json sets `runtime_disambiguation` to false, so Stage 02 did not instrument the workspace; the chain is closed from staged source, patch, saved ASan traces, reproduction_report.json, and direct inspection of the staged poc bytes alone.

The saved artifacts prove that the outer alternate translator differed from `"en"` because nested `SetTranslator2("en")` executed the `strcmp(new_language, translator2_language) != 0` delete branch, but they do not name that exact alternate language string; the causal chain does not require it.

coarse_trace.summary: `Synthesize()` decodes the witness into `p_decoder`; `ReadClause()` pulls those characters through `GetC()` into the clause buffer; `TranslateClause()` tokenizes the clause into `sbuf`/`words[]` and selects the attacker-controlled word.
The first translation of that selected word emits `phonSWITCH`, so `TranslateWord2()` allocates or selects global `translator2` for a different language.
The same word is retranslated under `tr == translator2`; a later non-alphabetic character in that word has no rule match and falls into `LookupLetter()`'s normal-text fallback path.
The nested English fallback reuses global `translator2` by calling `SetTranslator2("en")` while the outer translation still holds that same translator.
Because the requested language differs from the outer alternate translator, `SetTranslator2()` deletes the live `translator2` object and clears the global.
Control returns to the outer `TranslateRules()` loop, which keeps using stale `tr` and crashes on `tr->groups2_count[c]` with the saved ASan heap-use-after-free READ.

fine_trace.note: Source step. `Synthesize()` consumes the fuzzer-provided UTF-8/SSML buffer and materializes it into shared decoder state `p_decoder`. `SpeakNextClause()` later drives clause translation by pulling characters back out of this decoder.

`ReadClause()` seeds its clause-reading loop by fetching the next decoded codepoint from `p_decoder` through `GetC()`. `GetC()` itself returns `text_decoder_getc(p_decoder)` at line 174, so this is the decoder-to-clause handoff.

As the loop advances, `ReadClause()` writes each fetched character into `buf` and records its source position in `charix`, materializing the attacker-controlled clause text that `TranslateClause()` will later scan and tokenize.

While scanning `source` into `sbuf`, `TranslateClause()` turns unsupported non-alpha punctuation into spaces unless the character is in `tr->punct_within_word`. The default translator initializes `punct_within_word` to only apostrophe (`tr_languages.c:214,274`), so punctuation in the witness can split word boundaries before translation.

When a separator is reached, `TranslateClause()` finalizes the current token by appending a space in `sbuf` and recording that word's source offset and length in `words[]`. This preserves which attacker-controlled span from the clause buffer will later be treated as a word.

For the current clause iteration, `TranslateClause()` selects one tokenized attacker-controlled span as `word`. This pointer, not the raw original byte suffix, is what the downstream translation logic processes.

The first translation of the selected `word` produces a `phonSWITCH` directive instead of finishing in the base translator, and `TranslateWord2()` materializes the alternate-language string in `new_language`. This is the first attacker-derived state that makes the later translator lifetime bug possible.

`TranslateWord2()` selects or allocates global `translator2` for that alternate language. The ASan allocation stack ties the later-stale translator object back to this call path through `SetTranslator2 -> SelectTranslator -> NewTranslator`.

The same attacker-controlled word is retransmitted through `TranslateWord()` with `tr == translator2`. The outer translation now holds a live alias to the heap translator object selected in the previous step.

During this outer `TranslateRules(tr == translator2, ...)` call, a later non-alphabetic character in the same word has no matching pronunciation rule, so the normal-text fallback sends that character and the live `tr` alias into `LookupLetter()`.

Nested fallback step. `LookupLetter()` probes English for that character by reusing the same global `translator2` slot, even though the outer translation is still holding `tr == translator2`. The staged patch changes this nested fallback to `SetTranslator3("en")` instead.

Root-cause step. The nested English fallback enters `SetTranslator2()` while `translator2` still points at the outer alternate translator, and the different language request takes the delete branch. AddressSanitizer's free stack shows the free at line 1283; clearing `translator2` here invalidates the outer `tr` alias that `TranslateRules()` is still using.

After `LookupLetter()` returns, the outer `TranslateRules()` loop resumes on the same attacker-derived word and immediately reads through `tr`. Because the prior step already freed the translator object behind that alias, this dereference becomes the saved AddressSanitizer heap-use-after-free READ of size 1.

poc.trigger: PYTHONPATH=gt_generation python3 -m gt_toolkit arvo-workspace --result-dir /mnt/datastore/gt_generation/gt_results/arvo_42500437 run --version vulnerable --expect crash

format.name: espeak-ng UTF-8/SSML text
format.contract: The input must still be accepted as UTF-8 text under `espeakCHARS_UTF8 | espeakPHONEMES | espeakSSML` and, after `TranslateClause()` tokenization, present an attacker-controlled word that first makes `TranslateWord2()` produce `phonSWITCH` to a non-English alternate translator, then later in that same retranslation makes `LookupLetter()` call `SetTranslator2("en")`; that nested reuse of `translator2` is the minimal witnessed trigger for the UAF.
